content: The document titled Framework for the Evaluation of New Tests for Tuberculosis Infection was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2020. It is available in both electronic and print versions, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-000718-5 and 978-92-4-000719-2. The suggested citation for this document is: Framework for the Evaluation of New Tests for Tuberculosis Infection. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2020. The document acknowledges contributions from various experts and organizations, including the Research Institute of Tuberculosis in Japan, the University of Brescia in Italy, the New Diagnostics Working Group of the Stop TB Partnership, the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND), McGill University in Canada, and the WHO Global TB Programme. The technical working group used a consensus-building process to develop the document, which was informed by a non-systematic review of previous studies and protocols. The background section highlights that approximately one-quarter of the global population is estimated to be infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Individuals with this infection are at risk of progressing to active tuberculosis (TB) disease, with a lifetime risk of 5–15%, peaking within the first two years after infection. The risk of progression varies based on host factors such as comorbidities, age, and nutritional status. Treating TB infection, also known as tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), is a critical component of the End TB Strategy (2016–2035). At the 2018 United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB, member states committed to providing TPT to at least 30 million people by 2022, including 6 million people living with HIV, 4 million children under 5 years old who are household contacts of TB patients, and 20 million other household contacts. Currently, there is no gold-standard method for diagnosing TB infection. WHO recommends the use of the tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) to identify candidates for TPT. These tests measure immune sensitization to M. tuberculosis, but a positive result does not necessarily indicate the presence of live TB bacilli. Consequently, these tests may remain positive even after successful TPT. While these tests are useful for identifying individuals at higher risk of developing TB, they have limited predictive value for progression from infection to active disease. Less than 10% of individuals with a positive test develop TB disease within two years. Therefore, the development and evaluation of tests with higher predictive capacity are a research priority. WHO published target product profiles for such tests in 2017, emphasizing the need for tests with at least 90% sensitivity and specificity for predicting TB disease development. Until such advanced tests become available, TST and IGRA remain the standard tests for TB infection. However, in high-burden countries, testing is not required before starting TPT for high-priority groups, such as people living with HIV and household contacts under five years old. For other at-risk populations, testing is recommended to identify those who would benefit most from treatment and to avoid unnecessary medication. Challenges in implementing TB infection tests include high costs (for IGRA), cold-chain requirements (for TST), limited supply of quality-assured TST, and inadequate laboratory infrastructure for IGRA testing in decentralized settings. These challenges underscore the need for new tests with better operational characteristics. The document outlines the principles for evaluating new tests for TB infection, aiming to standardize evaluation processes and accelerate the adoption of new tests into global and national policies. It provides guidance on study designs, evaluation protocols, and operational and performance characteristics of tests. However, it does not prescribe specific thresholds for diagnostic performance or minimum requirements for new tests. The development of the document involved a technical expert group established by WHO in November 2019. This group included experts from WHO, the Stop TB Partnership, FIND, and McGill University. The draft document was developed through in-person and virtual meetings and was reviewed by an ad hoc expert committee before finalization. The framework for evaluating new tests for TB infection emphasizes diagnostic and predictive performance, laboratory characteristics (e.g., analytical sensitivity, precision), and other critical aspects.
